en: The Mahāyāna Treatise on the Refutation of Existence,
composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven during the Chao-feng era, the Great [Master].

The Imperial Envoy, the Minister for the Promotion of Light and Virtue, the Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, the Purple-Garbed Subject Shi Hu, respectfully translates by imperial decree: I take refuge in all Buddhas!
O you who possess wisdom, you should understand all phenomena as they truly are.
What is meant here? It means that all natures arise from the absence of nature (*abhāva*), yet they do not arise from the absence of nature.
If all natures were to have an arising, then those natures would be eternal.
This nature is without reality, like a flower in the sky; one should know that all phenomena are equal to empty space.
The arising of those phenomena is also equal to emptiness; all conditioned dharmas are like empty space, and since they lack reality, how could they possibly exist?
All phenomena are without cause and likewise without fruit; furthermore, no self-nature of karma can be apprehended, for herein nothing at all possesses reality.
Since there is no mundane world, there is no supramundane world; everything is unborn and devoid of intrinsic nature—how, then, could any phenomena arise?

The worldly affection between father and son or among kinsmen, though they are born, lacks any reality; for they do not arise from what was produced in a previous life, nor do they possess any inherent characteristics in the present life.
In this world, nothing meaningful can arise; it is like seeing various reflections within the moon.

The world lacks reality and arises from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); because of this conceptual construction, the mind of conceptualization arises. With this mind as its cause, the body comes into being; therefore, the embodied self moves about in the world.

Because it is composed of the aggregates (*skandha*), it is called a "body. All aggregates are empty and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); since the aggregates lack intrinsic nature, they are also without mind. Because there is no mind, there is therefore no body.

One should know that intrinsic nature is free from all conceptual discrimination; if there is no mind, there are no phenomena, and if there is no body, there are no realms. What is taught herein is the non-dual path; what is taught herein is the teaching of ultimate reality.

In this, all things are free from objects of perception; that which is spoken of here is free from objects of perception; that which is practiced here is free from objects of perception; and that which is attained here is free from objects of perception.

By constantly practicing all dharmas—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—in this manner, one will be able to realize unsurpassed bodhi before long.

Abiding in the limit of reality through the skillful means of wisdom, one gives rise to compassionate conduct to extensively deliver sentient beings; yet, although there is thus the appearance of something attained, the nature of omniscience cannot be said to be attained.

All those phenomena exist as mere names; all abide only within the realm of conceptualization. They arise from no real, manifest differentiation, and yet the phenomena that arise through differentiation do not truly exist.

All those phenomena are fundamentally without names; they are merely expressed through conventional designations. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena lack substantial reality and that everything arises from conceptual discrimination.
In this regard, if there were no conceptualization, it would be identical to space, free from all conceptualization.
To say that "the eye can see forms" is a statement of ultimate truth.

In this world, there are those with minds of false attachment who grasp what has been taught as being according to reality; whatever appears as a collection or category of phenomena, know that such teaching is the word of the Buddha.
Therefore, one should know that the meaning herein is that the eye does not see forms, and so on, up to the mind which does not cognize phenomena.
If one knows thus, such a person is a wise one who is able to penetrate the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this is what is called the supreme reality.
I have now provided this brief exposition according to the sūtras.
This concludes the Mahāyāna Treatise on the Refutation of Existence.
